To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
NZB and NZB mice have defects in hematopoietic differentiation which are not linked genetically to the genes which control autoantibody production.
1) The defect in NZC mice is in the recipient microenvironment and is controlled by a recessive gene which is not linked to either the H-2 or agouti locus.
the NZB and NZB/NZC mouse strains have two independent genetic defects that result in hematopoietic disorders.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the genetic analysis of the defects in hematopoietic differentiation in the NZB and NZB mice.
the study of the development of autoimmunity in the New Zealand Black mouse.
two aspects of stem cell differentiation in NZB and related mice: 1) the genetic analysis of stem cell differentiation, and 2) the genetic analysis and control of autoantibody production.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the NZC mice show a defect in the environment of the spleen that renders them incapable of supporting transplanted CFUs to form colonies, whereas NZB mice show a defect at the level of the CFU.
in the NZB mouse the defect in stem cell differentiation is in the CFU cell itself, whereas in the NZC mouse it is in the microenvironment of the spleen.
in NZC mice the microenvironment of the spleen is abnormal and in NZB mice the stem cell population itself is abnormal.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the NZB and NZB × NZC mice are useful for studying the genetic control and the molecular events of the early stages of hematopoietics differentiation, and that the latter is independent of the genetic factors controlling the autoantibody response to red cells in these mice.
the NZB mouse is a model of an auto-immune disease, but that the NZC mouse is not.
the NZB and NZB × NZC mice have an elevated endogenous CFUCFU-S count, and that NZC mice show a defect in the ability to allow normal CFU activity in their spleens.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the NZB and NZB/W mice have an intrinsic abnormality of hematopoiesis, which is not linked to the autoimmune disease.
NZC mice show a defect in the ability of the microenvironment of the spleen to support CFU activity.
there are at least two separate defects in NZB mice that affect the hematopoietic system.
